title: Iran chose to restart the fight after the US stopped – and showed a new appetite for risk
description: Iran has brought days of relative calm in the Middle East to an end after launching what the US called a “surprise” attack in a striking change to the pattern of fighting.
fullText:
Iran has brought days of relative calm in the Middle East to an end after launching what the US called a "surprise" attack in a striking change to the pattern of fighting.

Rather than responding to a fresh American strike, Tehran chose to restart the fight itself, showing a growing willingness to use military force to shape the course of the war on its own terms.

This in turn sets the stage for fresh escalation. "We are going to beat the f**king sh*t out of them," US President Donald Trump told Fox News Wednesday morning. "We'll be hitting them hard. They're going to get a beating."

That threat could hardly have surprised Tehran, which launched its missiles knowing they might bring US bombers back.

Trump had attributed last week's pause to a request from Iran because "they asked us very nicely" and wanted talks. Tehran never publicly committed to the recent pause, although a senior Iranian official said "our armed forces also decided not to take military action."

That makes Iran's decision to resume fire all the more significant.

Hours after publicly signaling that it would match the US restraint, Tehran targeted American forces – apparently deciding that raising the pressure was worth the risk of restarting the nightly bombardment.

"Something appears to have changed fundamentally in Iran's approach, particularly regarding its willingness to initiate a strike if it considers that to be the only viable option," Hamid Reza Azizi, a researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X.

Iran's strike came soon after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's meeting with Trump in Washington, DC, which the Israeli leader described as "one of the best conversations" the two have had following growing friction between the pair. Hours before the meeting, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Israel had wanted to strike Iranian energy infrastructure but had been held back by the Trump administration.

"The attack appears to have been a signal related to Netanyahu's visit to the White House earlier in the day," wrote Azizi. "It suggests that Iran's military strategy may have changed and that Tehran is now prepared to launch a preemptive strike if it detects signs of an imminent threat."

Shortly after the attack in Jordan, the US and Saudi militaries jointly struck Iran-backed militias in Iraq. US Central Command framed the Iraq operation not as retaliation for the Jordan attack, but as a response to more than 30 drone attacks against US forces and Saudi energy infrastructure over the previous 72 hours.

The overnight escalation showed how the war is widening. Saudi Arabia, long wary of being pulled directly into the conflict, is becoming more deeply involved as it faces threats on three fronts: the Houthis in Yemen, Iran-backed militias in Iraq, and Iran itself.

"The central challenge facing Washington and its Gulf partners is that neither Iran nor its regional allies appear willing to retreat from what they now define as core strategic objectives," Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a former head of the Iran branch in Israeli military intelligence, wrote on X.

"Tehran continues to insist on maintaining its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, while the Houthis have made clear that they will not end their campaign unless the Saudi-led (blockade) imposed on them (is) lifted."

In an interview with Iranian state television published just hours before the attack in Jordan, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi offered perhaps one of the clearest articulations of Tehran's position yet. Iran had stopped firing, he suggested, but would not hesitate to resume hostilities if its claim of sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz was challenged.

Tehran could not consider itself victorious if the strait returned to its prewar status, the deputy foreign minister said. The waterway had become central to the country's national security and a "defensive tool."

When the interviewer asked why Tehran had risked restarting the war by attacking commercial ships despite a functioning ceasefire, Gharibabadi said Iran regarded efforts by Oman and the US to establish a rival shipping route through the strait as a red line. Allowing that route to operate, he argued, would have reduced Iran's claim to the "effective exercise of sovereignty" over the waterway to "nothing more than a fantasy."

"One might look at it simply and ask why Iran would hit three commercial ships with missiles just because they turned off their GPS, potentially restarting a war," he said. "But if you look behind the scenes, you see that the arrangements applied to the Strait of Hormuz will have a long-term impact on the security of the Islamic Republic of Iran."

From Tehran's perspective, Washington's pause in attacks on Iran reflects "strategic weakness rather than restraint," Citrinowicz wrote. That perception risks fueling a cycle in which Iran escalates to impose greater costs, while neither side backs down for fear of losing credibility.

The US and its partners therefore face a choice, he argued: accommodate some Iranian demands, or accept the prospect of a prolonged conflict marked by mounting attacks on shipping, energy infrastructure and trade routes.

Aida Karimi, Eyad Kourdi, Dana Karni, Mohammed Tawfeeq and Tal Shalev contributed to this report.

title: CNN Poll: Americans doubt Trump is paying enough attention to the country’s most important problems
description: A record-high 73% of US adults say that President Donald Trump hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds, with just 27% saying he’s ...
fullText:
A record-high 73% of US adults say that President Donald Trump hasn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems, a new CNN poll conducted by SSRS finds, with just 27% saying he's had the right priorities.

That comes amid increasingly bleak views of the Iran war, stagnating economic unhappiness, and broad discontent about Trump's approach to these challenges.

Roughly two-thirds of Americans think that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions and that his military decisions in Iran have hurt the US. Around three-quarters say the president is not in touch with the problems ordinary Americans face in their daily lives.

Trump's overall approval rating, 34%, matches the career low he last saw at the close of his first term, following the January 6, 2021, insurrection. Half of Americans now strongly disapprove of him, a high across his terms, with a record-low 15% strongly approving.

Within his own party, his approval rating has hit a new low at 78% among Republicans, and just 19% of Republicans say they're enthusiastic about the rest of his second term, down from 38% last spring.

While his ratings are underwater across a range of issues tested, Trump sees his lowest numbers on a trio of interconnected issues: Just 28% approve of his handling of the situation in Iran, 25% on inflation and 21% on gas prices, with significant pockets of disapproval even among his supporters.

With an increasing majority of Americans anticipating a long-term military conflict, only about one-quarter think Trump has a clear plan for handling the situation, down from 40% at the start of the war. And 62% now say Trump is not an effective world leader, up from 54% who felt that way early in his second term.

Just one-quarter now say the war has been worth the toll in American lives and dollars, with younger Americans particularly skeptical.

On the most tangible economic fallout of the conflict in Iran, 74% of Americans say rising gas prices have caused them at least some hardship, up from 63% in March, with just under one-quarter believing the president has a plan to address the issue. And 71% say Trump hasn't gone far enough in trying to reduce the price of everyday goods, up from 58% a year ago.

There are few domestic bright spots for the president, whose issue approval ratings top out at 41% for handling voting rights and election integrity – one topic where his supporters have rallied most closely around him. Just 39% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of immigration, a relative positive at the start of his second term, with 35% approving of his management of the federal government.

Following two recent deadly ICE shootings, Americans say by a 20-point margin that the agency is making cities less, not more, safe. And amid the cyclospora outbreak and a surge in measles cases, they say by a 34-point margin that changes to health agencies like the FDA and CDC are leaving the public less, not more, safe.

Trump has never gotten high marks in polling as someone who's in touch with the problems of ordinary Americans. In the latest poll, just 27% say that description applies to him, while about two-thirds say that he's someone who does not put the good of the country ahead of his personal gain.

Those numbers reflect broad skepticism about the high-profile projects that would leave Trump's mark on the nation's capital. A 58% majority of Americans say they feel dissatisfied or angry about the construction projects Trump has undertaken in Washington, DC, including the effort to build a new White House ballroom and renovate the Reflecting Pool. Just 17% express positive feelings, with another 25% saying it doesn't matter to them.

At the time of Trump's second inauguration, nearly half of Americans thought it was at least somewhat likely that Trump would avoid conflicts between his family's company and his work as president, but a scant 23% think he's done so at least somewhat well. And 57% say it's a bad thing that Trump earned more than $2 billion last year while serving as an elected official, including income from cryptocurrency holdings, royalty payments and property investments. Just 7% see that as a good thing, with 36% calling his earnings while president something that doesn't matter much.

More than 6 in 10 say that Trump has gone too far in pursuing his personal business interests while serving as president and undertaking projects to remodel the White House and other Washington landmarks, with nearly as many saying he's gone too far in making changes to cultural institutions like the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian.

These efforts aren't even very popular among the president's base. Only 43% of Republicans say they feel positively about Trump's construction projects, with 35% saying that the projects don't matter to them. And most Republicans say that his earnings as president are irrelevant, with those who do hold an opinion more likely to see it as a negative than a positive.

CNN's Jennifer Agiesta and Edward Wu contributed to this report.

title: You Can Now Let Gemini 'See' Your Mac's Display for Free
description: You can let Gemini understand your screen and take action on your behalf.
fullText:
It may be polarizing, but there are lot of people using AI right now. Most of those users are likely exclusive to a chatbot, like ChatGPT or Gemini, using it as a Google replacement (don't do that), or as a confidant (please don't do that either). But if your goal is to use AI as a personal assistant, listen up: On Wednesday, Google announced two new updates for Gemini on macOS, one of which may have some privacy and security implications for users—assuming they opt in to it.

If you use dictation on macOS (i.e., speaking words out loud and having the AI type them for you), you might have a reason to use Gemini over Apple's built-in solutions. Going forward, Gemini on macOS has "intelligent dictation," which Google says polishes text "instantly at the cursor." That means Gemini will remove your stammers, like "ums" and "ahs" in between words, things you never would type out yourself. This works in any window on your Mac: You just press the Fn key, and start speaking.

We'll have to see this feature in action to know how well it works, but it does build off of similar enhancements Gemini has on other platforms. It's a small adjustment, but one that will make it possible to use Gemini to draft texts, emails, or documents without having to totally self-edit. That's the kind of utility I'm looking for from AI features. And since it's enabled by default, everyone using Gemini on Mac will be using it—unless they dig into their settings to turn it off.

Google's second update for Gemini on macOS isn't so straightforward, nor is it enabled by default. Google calls it "screen-aware reasoning," a feature that grants Gemini permission to "understand" what's happening on your Mac's screen. The idea is to hand tasks over to Gemini: If you have your Notes app open, for example, you could press the Fn key and say "Turn these notes into an executive summary for the meeting this afternoon." Gemini will reportedly know to look at your Notes app, analyze your text, and configure it on your behalf, all without needing to work through a proprietary app.

You can stack together a series of commands, too: You could ask Gemini to draft an email for a team dinner, and pull from a select group of files on your Mac for important info (participants, budget requirements, dietary restrictions, etc.) You could continue on, asking Gemini to search Google Maps for specific types of restaurants, and include them as options for the team. And at any point, you can correct yourself, and Gemini will adjust accordingly. For example, if you said the team dinner should be at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, but later on in your command you say, "Sorry, dinner should be 7 p.m." Gemini should make the appropriate changes.

Sure, there's a usefulness to this type of feature. If you're already using Gemini on macOS, letting "see" your Mac's display makes it more helpful. Rather than rely on the Gemini app for all your tasks, you can expand its range to your whole Mac, and, if Google is correct, in quite a complex way. But there's always a privacy risk in allowing AI programs full access to what's happening on your personal computer, and perhaps a security risk as well. Do you want Google's AI to be able to see everything on your screen?

It's not as big a risk as a true agentic program, of course. If you pay for Google's most expensive AI plan, you can access Gemini Spark, which can run autonomously on your Mac. The biggest flag to note is "prompt injection," in which hackers hide malicious commands for your AI in websites. If you task the AI to do something, and it stumbles upon such a command, it will think the request comes from you, not from the hacker. So, when it processes a request like "open [malicious site] and download [malicious file]" it will without question; or "open [crypto wallet], log in with saved credentials, and send funds to [account]," it will follow suit. That shouldn't be an issue with Gemini as it stands, though it theoretically could, if you ask it to perform a task that exposes it to prompt injection.

If you're someone who is interested in the latest features, this isn't to dissuade you from using Gemini's new agentic feature on macOS, but it's worth considering the very real risks before you do.

title: How to Make Sure Your Claude Chats Don't Get Shared Publicly (Again)
description: Claude might've shared your chats on Google, but you can avoid that in the future.
fullText:
If you use Claude, Anthropic's AI chatbot, you might be aware that your chats may have been exposed on Google. The news broke over the weekend, as Redditors discovered a treasure trove of conversations between Claude users and their AI bots. All one had to do was search for a keyword followed by "site:claude.ai/share" to find Claude conversations about that topic. It was, to be frank, quite the mess.

Luckily, Anthropic quickly plugged the security hole. Ever since, searching Google with "site:claude.ai/share" returns no results, so you can't find any of these chats today if you try. However, it's not necessarily a huge comfort to know that Google indexed these conversations in the first place—and for the second time in a year, at that. Anthropic dealt with a similar situation back in September, and while it isn't alone—Google once also indexed ChatGPT conversations—you might understandably be concerned about future chats leaking onto the web, as well as wonder whether your current chats were exposed.

The thing is, it doesn't seem like every Claude chat had an equal risk of exposure here. Anthropic is adamant it doesn't share chat links to Google directly; instead, the vast majority (if not the entirety) of these chats appear to be conversations that individuals decided to share with others on the open web, according to Google. Claude lets you share your chats publicly if you wish, and while that can be convenient for showing friends, family, or colleagues a specific discussion, it might also open up your chat to Google's web crawlers, as when you share a chat, it generates a public link.

So, there's a silver lining in that private Claude chats that weren't shared are unlikely to be involved in this latest exposure. If you don't share your chats with anyone, you should be in the clear—though Futurism did report that one user in September's Claude debacle swears they never shared their exposed chats. However, if you do share Claude chats, your conversations might have been part of the indexing that happened over the weekend.

Further complicating things, it seems that Claude's "artifacts" are still visible on Google. Claude generates artifacts when the content of your project meets certain criteria, and can include anything like documents, code snippets, HTML sites, SVG images, diagrams, flowcharts, and Interactive React components. In many cases, users may want these artifacts to be public, as they may be meant to be shared widely. However, if you don't want your artifacts indexed on Google, you'll have to take action.

While there doesn't appear to be any reliable way to identify whether your chats and artifacts were included in this exposure, you can ensure that none of them are ever indexed by a search engine in the future. To do so, you'll essentially have to shut down sharing.

To start, head to Settings > Privacy in Claude, then choose "Manage" next to "Shared chats." Once this new page appears, you'll see all shared chats, including a link to the conversation and the date shared. From here, scroll through the list and select "Unshare" next to each chat you'd like to remove. This won't delete your chats; only their snapshots connected to these public links.

title: How to Stop Scammers From Showing You Ads on Your Android After Every Phone Call
description: It's a ad abuse scheme known as "AfterCall."
fullText:
If you're an Android user who is seeing ads pop up after your phone calls, you need not assume this is some new feature you have to learn to live with. It's actually an ad fraud scam, and you can do something about it. Researchers have identified dozens of apps on the Google Play Store that are able to display ads on top of the Android phone interface, a scheme known as AfterCall.

This scam originates with seemingly harmless utility apps downloaded from the Google Play Store, such as calendars, alarm clocks, and notepads. When installed, they request overlay permissions, which allow them to appear on top of other apps—and thus display ads over phone calls. These apps can detect when a call ends and will then launch full-screen ads wrapped in a fake call info screen. Since it looks like they are simply part of the call interface, users may be less likely to suspect that they are actually malicious.

It's worth noting that overlay permissions can't be granted via a standard pop-up during the app installation process. They are a type of "special permission" that requires users to go into their system settings to enable. Android apps are supposed to request these permissions in context and give a clear reason for doing so. AfterCall scammers are using justifications like alarms not being able to go off or appear correctly without overlay permissions, though some apps will simply crash if users decline permissions.

Because the ads appear out of context—after a phone call and with content unrelated to the utility app—it's harder for users to figure out what's causing them. The utility apps aren't obviously malicious and don't appear on recent app lists when ads are displayed, so it's not obvious that they are connected to the problem.

If you are seeing ads pop up after phone calls on your Android, check for apps that have overlay permissions. Go to Settings > Apps > Special app access (this may be hidden behind a three-dot menu) and click on the permission type. Look for apps you don't recognize, or which shouldn't have "display on top" permissions, and uninstall them. You should regularly audit these permissions, and disable any that aren't essential.

On the user side, these apps seem to be mostly an annoyance rather than outright malicious programs that are harvesting your sensitive data, though installing any program that requests unnecessary permissions can introduce significant risk. If nothing else, however, these apps do appear to waste brands' advertising dollars and could damage their reputation with users—but you probably just care about how to stop seeing them after your calls.

title: McCartney wins breaststroke bronze in Glasgow
description: Northern Ireland's Ellie McCartney wins a bronze medal in the women's 200m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
Northern Ireland's Ellie McCartney has won a bronze medal in the women's 200m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

McCartney, 21, finished third behind home favourite Abgharad Evans and Kaylene Corbett of South Africa.

The 21-year-old had posted the sixth-fastest time in the semi-finals but put in a storming performance to take third in a time of 2:24.73.

Her time was enough to win bronze ahead of Australia's Ella Ramsay by 0.16 seconds.

McCartney is Commonwealth Youth Games in 2023 and European Under-23 gold medallist last year, but her bronze in Glasgow is a first senior international medal for the Enniskillen swimmer.

It is a third medal in the pool for Northern Ireland after Bethany Firth's bronze medal in the 200m freestyle S14 and Barry McClements' silver in the men's S9 100m backstroke.

Gary Kelly and the duo of Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill won bronze medals in bowls, and four Northern Ireland boxers are guaranteed medals.

In the men's 200m freestyle, Jack McMillan finished in sixth place as Kai Taylor of Australia won gold.

James Guy was second and Matt Richard took bronze.

McMillan was second after 100m metres but a surge from his Team GB team-mates was enough to surpass the 26-year-old and he finished in a time of 1:46.29 seconds.

Olympic 800m champion Daniel Wiffen will compete in the men's 1500m freestyle at 20:50 BST as he looks to win his first medal of the Games.

title: Neville joins Charlton as Leicester sign Irish duo
description: Charlton Athletic have signed full-back Ashleigh Neville from Leicester City on a two-year deal.
fullText:
Charlton Athletic have signed full-back Ashleigh Neville from Leicester City on a two-year deal.

The 33-year-old has made over 100 appearances in the Women's Super League and brings a wealth of experience to newly-promoted Charlton.

Neville also reunites with manager Karen Hills, who she spent three years working with at Tottenham as they earned promotion to the top-flight.

"It's an exciting journey for myself and the club so I'm really happy to be here," said Neville.

"I know what Karen's about and she knows what I bring. I'm really looking forward to working with her again.

"I'm hoping I can bring experience from the WSL and to bring things on and off the pitch with the way I play."

Full-back Neville joined Leicester on a one-and-a-half-year deal in January but the Foxes were relegated following defeat by Charlton in a play-off in May.

It is believed there was no release clause in her contract relating to relegation and a mutual termination was not agreed so a fee was likely paid by Charlton.

Meanwhile, Leicester have signed Republic of Ireland internationals Jessie Stapleton and Jessica Ziu for undisclosed fees from West Ham.

It is believed versatile defender Stapleton, 21, has joined on a three-year deal while midfielder Ziu, 24, has signed a two-year contract.

Stapleton, who can also play in midfield, struggled to break into West Ham's team, instead enjoying loan spells at Reading, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest.

"I'm happy it's over the line and I'm excited to get going. This is a club with a lot of ambition," said Stapleton.

"The club can help me grow as a player and I feel I can help the club get back to where it belongs."

Ziu spent four years at West Ham and made 23 appearances, as well as spending six months on loan at Bristol City for the first half of last season.

"The plan and structure the club has in place is really exciting. I can't wait to get the jersey on and play in front of all the fans at King Power Stadium," said Ziu.

title: MI London hold out in nail-biting tie with Spirit
description: MI London hold London Spirit to a nail-biting tie at The Oval after Hayley Matthews concedes only three runs from the last three balls of the match.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, The Oval

MI London 151-4 (100 balls): Kerr 49* (32); Kapp 2-24

London Spirit (151-5 balls): Jones (49); Gordon 2-29, Matthews 2-33

MI London held London Spirit to a nail-biting tie at The Oval after Hayley Matthews conceded only three runs from the last three balls of the match.

With Spirit needing nine off the final set, Matthews' international team-mate Deandra Dottin struck a four off the first ball before adding a single from the following delivery.

Matthews struck back, having Nadine de Klerk caught at deep mid-wicket for 13 and keeping new batter Charlie Dean to a single.

Dottin was only able to chop Matthews' final delivery into the leg side, scrambling through for two as the two sides played out their second tie in three years.

The south London franchise, who secured their first points of the season after losing their opening three matches, reached 151-4 after being put into bat.

Melie Kerr struck an unbeaten 49 from 32 balls from number three, putting on 46 with captain Hollie Armitage (23) and an unbroken stand of 54 with Chinelle Henry, who hit two fours and two sixes in a 12-ball 33.

Henry then had big-hitting opener Grace Harris caught by Armitage off the first ball of the reply, but Amy Jones steadied the Spirit innings.

The visiting wicketkeeper also top-scored with 49, with her total coming from 36 balls, putting on partnerships of 68 with Marie Kelly (45) and 51 with Marizanne Kapp (25).

Spirit looked well set, needing 33 from 26 balls, before they lost Jones and Kapp within the space of four deliveries.

Kapp top-edged Matthews to Dani Gregory immediately after hitting a six, while Jones swept Kirstie Gordon to Nicola Carey at backward square straight after hitting four through the covers.

MI kept themselves in the hunt, conceding 19 off the next 17 balls, setting up the dramatic final set which saw Spirit finish on 151-5.

The home side move off the bottom of the table, with their two points taking them above Birmingham Phoenix on net run-rate.

Spirit rise above Welsh Fire and Sunrisers Leeds to sit fourth, with a win, a defeat and a tie from their three matches.

Brave's men, meanwhile, will be eyeing their first win of the season in the match that follows at 18.30.

title: Duckett leads Rockets to convincing win over Fire
description: Trent Rockets demolish Welsh Fire by nine wickets in Cardiff to make it two wins from three matches in this season's Hundred.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Sophia Gardens

Welsh Fire 122-7 (100 balls): Short 36 (26); Santner 3-35

Trent Rockets 126-1 (72 balls): Duckett 52* (45), Allen 33 (19)

Trent Rockets won by nine wickets

Ben Duckett struck an unbeaten half-century as Trent Rockets demolished Welsh Fire by nine wickets in Cardiff to make it two wins from three matches in this season's Hundred.

Chasing 123 on a tricky two-paced wicket at Sophia Gardens, the visitors made a solid start through Duckett before Finn Allen picked up the pace with a rapid 33 from 19 balls during a 75-run opening partnership.

Allen eventually fell to Rachin Ravindra with Rockets needing 48 runs from 56 balls.

England opener Duckett, however, continued to build a cautious innings, reaching his seventh half-century in the competition's history in 43 balls.

Fire's task of defending a paltry total was not helped by the seven free hits their bowlers conceded and with Tom Banton adding a brisk unbeaten 31 from 15 balls, Rockets reached the target with 28 balls to spare.

The win sealed a double for Rockets over Fire on Wednesday after their women's side had also won comfortably earlier.

Batting first, Fire had huffed and puffed to 122-7 after losing Phil Salt and Joe Root early for single figures to Matt Henry's bowling.

Matt Short proved to be the only top-order batter to make a meaningful contribution for the home side with 36 from 26 balls.

New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner then sent back his compatriot Ravindra for 16 before Jordan Cox provided Fire with some late impetus.

Cox's knock of 33 from 16 balls included three consecutive sixes off Santner but the left-arm spinner accounted for his wicket from the very next delivery to finish with figures of 3-35.

Southern Brave face Birmingham Phoenix in Southampton on Thursday.

In the women's competition, the home side, who sit at the top of the table, will be aiming for a fourth win from as many matches, while Phoenix are yet to win after two games. They meet at 15:00 BST.

title: Ukraine appeal IOC decision to reinstate Russia
description: Ukraine's National Olympic Committee launches an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport against the International Olympic Committee's decision to provisionally reinstate Russia to its competitions.
fullText:
Ukraine's National Olympic Committee has launched an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport against the International Olympic Committee's decision to provisionally reinstate Russia to its competitions.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) suspended the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) in 2023 in response to the war in Ukraine but lifted the ban on 7 July 2026, stating it was "no longer applicable", external.

That decision opens the door for Russian athletes to compete for their country at the 2028 Olympic Games and is the latest step in the country's reinstatement to international competition, with the IOC previously recommending in December 2025 that federations readmit Russian and Belarusian Under-23 athletes.

However, the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Ukraine said the IOC's decision is "premature" and "violates" the Olympic Charter.

"The position of the NOC of Ukraine is based on the fact that the IOC's decision was made prematurely and without proper verification of whether the violations - which led to the suspension of the ROC following the appeal by the NOC of Ukraine on October 6, 2023 - had actually been resolved," an NOC statement said.

Russia could compete at LA 2028 Olympics

"The NOC of Ukraine also points out that as early as 2024, the Cas [Court of Arbitration for Sport] confirmed the legality of the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, recognising that the inclusion of sports organisations from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine violates the territorial integrity of the NOC of Ukraine and the provisions of the Olympic Charter," it continued.

"For this reason, the Ukrainian side believes that reinstating the ROC's rights without effectively addressing these violations is incompatible with the principles of international sports law and sets a dangerous precedent for the entire Olympic Movement."

Russian and Belarusian athletes competed as neutrals at the 2024 Olympics in Paris and 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina.

Russia remain banned by world football's governing body Fifa, while in May, World Athletics rejected a recommendation by the IOC to lift the ban on Belarusian athletes and teams.

title: England thrash Tonga to boost semi-final hopes
description: England break their Commonwealth Games record goals tally with a convincing 94-32 victory over Tonga.
fullText:
England broke their Commonwealth Games record goals tally with a convincing 94-32 victory over Tonga.

In a must-win Pool A game in their quest for a semi-final place, England raced into a 27-8 lead at the end of the first quarter and maintained their dominance throughout at the Hydro in Glasgow.

Knowing goal average and possibly goal difference could be crucial in the battle for a top-two spot, the 2018 champions were keen for a significant margin of victory.

They did just that by surpassing their previous record of 89 goals in one game in the competition, set against Sri Lanka in 2002.

Goal shooter Eleanor Cardwell - one of only two members of the 12-player squad with Commonwealth Games experience - made sure England kept their foot on the gas with 54 goals from her 60 attempts.

Meanwhile, goal attackers Sasha Glasgow (18) and Ella Clark (12) netted 30 times between them and Cardwell's second-quarter replacement Olivia Tchine chipped in with 10 goals.

Victory for England leaves them third in their pool but level on six points with South Africa and defending champions Australia, who face each other at 21:00 BST.

The Roses boosted their goal average to 1.74 and goal difference to 127, while South Africa's is 2.06 (GD 123) and Australia's is 1.99 (GD 116).

England will take on South Africa in a vital final group game in the race for the semi-final at 21:00 BST on Thursday.

Tonga, who have enjoyed a remarkable journey over the past 12 years to climb to eighth in the world rankings, are out of their first Commonwealth Games.

Commonwealth Games netball standings, external

Earlier, Scotland came agonisingly close to a huge upset in their Pool B game against Jamaica but fell just short, losing 45-43 in a thrilling contest.

Jamaica, who are ranked fourth in the world, beat Scotland 78–34 the last time they met at the Commonwealth Games in 2022.

Despite the fine margins, defeat for Scotland - ranked 10th - severely dented their hopes of reaching the last four.

They will need to beat Uganda by a big margin in their final game at 11:00 BST on Thursday and hope other results go their way to stand any chance of progressing.

Wales face 2022 bronze medallists New Zealand at 19:00 BST and must win to stand any chance of qualifying, though their campaign is also realistically over, barring a miracle set of results in which they would need to overturn a huge goal difference.

Northern Ireland's 78-30 defeat by South Africa in Pool A on Tuesday consigned them to a fourth straight loss, with their chances of qualifying for the semi-final already long gone.

title: Yize sets up Murphy rematch at Shanghai Masters
description: World champion Wu Yize knocks in three centuries as he beats Si Jiahui 6-2 in the second round of the Shanghai Masters.
fullText:
World champion Wu Yize struck three centuries as he beat Si Jiahui 6-2 in the second round of the Shanghai Masters.

In his first match of the season, Yize went 3-0 up before his Chinese compatriot pulled two frames back.

Yize responded by knocking in breaks of 108 and two 140s as he took three frames in a row for a victory which sets up a quarter-final against Shaun Murphy in a repeat of their thrilling 2026 World Championship final.

Murphy came through a tough battle with Zhou Yuelong before winning 6-5 as he struck a 65 to win the deciding frame.

"It was great to feel the enthusiasm from the crowd. It's been quite a while since I last played in front of fans like this," said Yize, 22.

"I also haven't really had the chance to practise properly recently, so when I got back out there I felt a little rusty at first.

"Fortunately, I managed to find my own rhythm and I think that was the key to winning today's match."

O'Sullivan knocked out of Shanghai Masters by Wilson

Zhao Xintong, the 2025 world champion, also hit three tons (112, 100 and 101) in his 6-2 win against fellow Chinese player Ding Junhui and will next play Neil Robertson.

Four-time world champion John Higgins edged past Jack Lisowski 6-5 to set up a last-eight tie against Judd Trump.

Lisowski knocked in a 123 and 109 to level the match at 5-5 before Higgins took the final frame on the black.

title: Welsh Rugby Union confirms Scarlets or Ospreys to be cut
description: The Welsh Rugby Union gives details of how it intends to cut a team - with Ospreys and Scarlets set to fight to be the side in south west Wales.
fullText:
The Welsh Rugby Union has outlined how it plans to cut from four professional teams to three by 2028, with Ospreys and Scarlets set to fight to be the side in south west Wales.

The governing body confirmed in April it intended to press on with plans to go down to three men's teams from the 2028-29 season, with one in the capital, one in the east and one in the west.

Cardiff, owned by the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU), and Dragons, an independently-backed business, are set to be given licences.

That would leave Swansea-based Ospreys and Llanelli-based Scarlets to compete for the remaining spot, with a merger also a practical, if controversial, possibility.

The WRU has stated that the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of the 2026-27 season.

"The WRU board has examined in detail a range of factors when determining the three future licence areas and has confirmed that only incumbent teams will be considered eligible for a licence," a WRU statement said.

"This means contingent on the agreement of the final licensing terms, Dragons RFC and Cardiff Rugby would be offered the respective east and capital licences."

Scarlets sign Wales fly-half Anscombe from Bayonne

High Court leaves rugby brain injury case in balance

Halfpenny commits coaching future to Cardiff

The WRU says it will bring together the leadership of all the professional teams, and other stakeholders, after Wales' Nations Championship matches in November.

It intends to thrash out the finances of the regions' proposals and assess the interests of the quartet in taking up the new licences.

"This will allow an orderly implementation and avoid prolonged uncertainty for clubs, players, supporters, investors and sponsors," said Marianne Okland, chair of Welsh rugby's Professional Rugby Board, whose members met on Monday.

"Assuming that Cardiff Rugby and Dragons RFC want to 

"We understand that there will be ongoing uncertainty until a final decision on the west licence is made.

"That is why we are committed to progressing in a collaborative way, whilst not underestimating the considerable challenges ahead, and providing stability for all at the earliest opportunity."

In April, the governing body confirmed that the cut to three teams would not happen until 2028 after a deal with Ospreys owners Y11 Sport & Media to buy Cardiff fell through.

Scarlets and Ospreys joined their eastern rivals in signing a Professional Rugby Agreement (PRA) this summer and are now poised to battle for survival.

That is unless they can be convinced or agree to merge, which was close to happening in 2019.

"We have already begun to put the support structures in place to develop the related player pathways, to create the best environments for our senior players, to provide the right financial support and to develop the facilities around them," said WRU vice chair John Manders.

"We are making important progress which will safeguard the future of our game, concentrate resources and give our teams the best chance of achieving success at all levels."

title: New mum Hall returns to scene of greatest triumph
description: Five months after giving birth to her son, Georgia Hall feels ready to return to  major stage at the course where she won the 2018 Women's Open.
fullText:
Following the safe arrival of her baby son, the next biggest date in Georgia Hall's diary comes this week as she returns to the scene of her greatest golfing triumph.

Aged just 22 and with her dad Wayne caddying, Hall won the 2018 AIG Women's Open in great style at Royal Lytham and St Annes. She remains the most recent British female player to win a major.

Now Hall, 30, is back on the Fylde coast, with five-month-old son Conor and the rest of her family in tow.

It was only when she first picked up a club again six weeks after giving birth that she entertained the idea of coming back to the venue that means so much to her.

"I was in Ireland and went to a local driving range," said Hall.

"I was really excited because I didn't know how I was going to hit it and thought I might top it or something.

"But I actually hit it pretty good, although there was no rotation at all. I went there for an hour and I was pleasantly surprised. I left thinking, 'OK, let's see if I can get back to Lytham.'"

Weeks later Hall returned to the Ladies European Tour, impressively making cuts in France, the Netherlands and Belgium. Those performances were enough to convince her she is ready to return to the major stage.

Hull & Woad provide hope for home Women's Open win

Korda & Hull seek major glory - Women's Open tee times

The ultimate achievement would be to now emulate her old Solheim Cup skipper Catriona Matthew, who won the Women's Open here at Lytham in 2009, just 11 weeks after giving birth to daughter Sophie.

The Scot plays down this remarkable achievement, saying it was easier than it would have been after the arrival of a first child.

"I spoke to her and I said, 'I really don't know how you did it,'" said Hall.

"You couldn't dream of doing that. I couldn't. She said, 'Oh, it's a lot easier with the second.'"

Hall asked for advice from Matthew, who told the Dorset star to manage expectations.

"Just as in expecting a little bit less, but not in a bad way," Hall told BBC Sport.

"If you hit a bad shot, you've been out of it for a year. You've given birth to a human.

"So it will take some time, basically be patient. And that's what I'm going to have in my mind this week."

Hall will marry Conor's father Paul Dunne, who led the 2015 Open as an amateur and beat Rory McIlroy to the 2017 British Masters title. The baby boy could hardly have more impeccable golfing genes.

And the new mum has already made sure of a family photo on the 18th green this week. Hall said: "It'll be my new screensaver."

Eight years ago the photos were of her clutching one of golf's most prestigious trophies, but that is not her abiding memory.

"I think just holing so many putts," she said.

"That's why you play golf. It wasn't even like holding the trophy at the end. It was the feeling you get from an accomplishment of holing great putts when it mattered.

"Just so many of them, I remember, and when I was playing practice rounds the last few days, I would remember, oh yeah, I hit it there and that pin position was there. So it is nice to relive."

It is probably asking too much this week for Hall to reprise that 2018 victory when she finished 17-under-par to win by two shots. This year the remodelled links is baked out, providing a fast, firm and fearsome challenge.

"Definitely it's one of the hardest," said Hall. "This golf course is so hard and they made changes that make it harder. So I'm expecting scoring to be a bit tricky.

"But I'm improving every month and that's just my only goal. I believe that my game's in decent shape and if I can get in the right mentality and hole some decent putts, I think I'll be OK."

title: Alalshikh investment in Derby County moves closer
description: Saudi Arabia government official Turki Al-Sheikh's investment deal into Derby County could be finalised as early as next week.
fullText:
Saudi Arabia government official Turki Alalshikh's investment deal into Derby County could be finalised as early as next week.

Alalshikh, co-founder of boxing promotion company Zuffa, is interested in buying a stake in the Championship club and there has been a deal on the table with English football's independent regulator since May.

With final checks set to take place, his investment is expected to be given the green light in the coming days, BBC Radio Derby reports.

The proposed deal had raised concerns among human rights campaigners, including Amnesty International, which last month said the independent regulator faced a "defining test" over the investment.

Alalshikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority - and someone who is close to the Kingdom's de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman - has been criticised by human rights groups for his role in alleged 'sportswashing'.

Saudi Arabia has been accused of using sports to improve its image in the wider world to distract from its human rights record, treatment of women, use of the death penalty and its anti-LGBT stance.

As well as being the owner of Egyptian club Pyramids between 2018 and 2019, Alalshikh recently owned Spanish side Almeria but sold the club to an investment group from Saudi Arabia last May.

The Independent Football Regulator, Derby County and Alalshikh have all declined to comment.

Dominic Dietrich, BBC Radio Derby

This is a story that has dominated the summer for Derby County since it was first revealed back in May.

It has now taken a big step forward as Turki Alalshikh looks set to make his first move into English football following a long-term desire to do so.

A number of interested parties have looked at the Rams since owner David Clowes first confirmed his willingness to take on extra investment upwards of 80%, with Clowes saying it has to be someone that can "accelerate" their progress to the Premier League.

The key in this development is the timeline - as we sit here on 29 July, the Rams have only brought in four players and have not made real steps forward so far in their recruitment to build on last season's impressive eighth-placed finish.

If this deal goes through next week as we expect, it will give Derby around three weeks to make an impact in the transfer window and strengthen their case for a play-off finish in the Championship, something head coach John Eustace will be desperate to achieve.

The questions that remain are how much investment Alalshikh will make, the percentages and exactly how this deal will be structured, but this may have just changed the trajectory for the Rams going forward.

title: Kerr and Wightman revel in Wednesday warm-up for mile final
description: Josh Kerr and Jake Wightman, both Scottish former world champions and rivals since they were boys, will race in the Commonwealth Games mile final.
fullText:
The men's mile final has long been slated as one of the defining moments of these Commonwealth Games. Josh Kerr and Jake Wightman just had to complete the formalites.

Saturday night will the big-ticket event of these 11 days in Glasgow. Wednesday morning was the pre-show. Both in the blue of Scotland. Two big men who have raced since they were wee boys in Edinburgh.

A bigger crowd than both expected turned up at Scotstoun in the west end of the city on a bright morning to watch the heats, which also included another world-class Scot in Neil Gourley.

Injury wrecked Gourley's chances of qualifying for the final in his home town, but double Olympic medallist Kerr, who has just set an astonishing new world record over this distance, and fellow former world champion Wightman did their bit in fine style.

Kerr cruised to victory in the first heat, surging and dropping for the first half of the race before pulling himself away from any danger to cross first. And Wightman eased to second spot in the following heat to set up Saturday's showdown.

One was showier than the other - Kerr beseeched the crowd to lift the volume at a couple of points in the final 200m - but both looked in fine fettle for what's to come.

"I had some time to pull in the crowd and work off their energy," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland.

"How many times in my career am I going to be running to the line in front of a world-class pack feeling as good as I am in front of a home crowd?

"People have spent their hard-earned money to come along here on a Wednesday morning and brought their kids along, so I just want to give them that bit of interaction and show that we're not robots.

"Many times I've come here and been third or fourth best to guys who really taught me how to run.

"I grew up dreaming of these championship and there's a nostalgia of my parents driving me down here at 12 years old and me getting well beaten and then driving home eating a sandwich."

Like Kerr, Wightman recalls his many races here from his youth and was overwhelmed by how much support there was for him, Kerr and Gourley.

"It was class," he said. "Wednesday morning felt like it had the potential to be one of the quieter sessions but it was electric.

"I've thought for a long time about what it would be like to win in front of a home crowd. Now I just have to go and do it."

title: Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?
description: BBC Sport explores why Fifa president Gianni Infantino feels powerful enough to sell off stakes in the World Cup - and what the consequences could be.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino is billing it as the democratisation of football.

But Fifa's announcement that it aims to sell off stakes in its football competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors via associates of US President Donald Trump has been met with incredulity and rage from fans, politicians and regional governing bodies.

The big selling point, according to Infantino, is $40m (£30m) in funding given to all Fifa countries to "develop the game" once the deal is finalised.

The Swiss has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (£15m).

This is the boldest move Infantino, an administrator who views himself as a world leader on par with presidents and prime ministers, has made in the decade since he became Fifa president.

If Fifa pushes the plan through, he will have consolidated his power for the long-term future and made investors wealthy along the way.

So why exactly does Infantino feel powerful enough to enact something so controversial, and what could the consequences be?

Infantino has enough support to suggest the plan is more likely to go ahead than not.

Since being elected Fifa president in 2016, Infantino has earned long-standing, widespread backing from many countries in Africa, Asia, and the Americas, which have gained financially from various policies he has managed.

They include the expansion of the World Cup to 48 teams, the growth in commercial and broadcast revenue Fifa has overseen, and a programme which allocates millions in funding directly to member countries every year.

That gives him a base of support which constitutes more than half of Fifa's 211 members.

Fifa votes require a simple majority - if more than half vote in favour, Infantino's plan will come into effect.

The proposal will appeal to many nations, particularly those lower down the football food chain, for whom a £15m windfall would be more than they would ordinarily make over several years.

The level of backing Infantino enjoys appears to have emboldened his approach to the presidency. Decisions such as the introduction of hydration breaks and a musical half-time show to the World Cup were taken by his administration without a vote of members, and would have been deemed unthinkable when he took charge a decade ago.

And his close relationship with Trump is key too.

The investment fund Fifa is dealing with - Thrive Capital - is led by Josh Kushner, the brother-in-law of Trump's daughter Ivanka.

Fifa says Greg Maffei, the American former president of Formula 1 owner Liberty Media who has donated to Trump's political campaigns in the past, is acting as a "key commercial advisor".

The proposal follows years of Infantino making overt attempts to deepen his and Fifa's ties with Trump.

He created a Peace Prize and awarded it to Trump. He opened a Fifa office in Trump Tower, New York. He allowed the Club World Cup trophy to be kept in the Oval Office at the White House. He laughed along during Trump's inauguration speech in which he threatened World Cup co-hosts Canada and Mexico.

And last week, Infantino heavily mimicked Trump's language when he released a statement describing those who criticised aspects of the organisation of the World Cup as "so consumed by hate and criticism".

Working with Trump associates on the plan allows Infantino to harness the power of the bond he has cultivated with the world's most powerful person, with the promise of a mutually beneficial outcome.

Fifa has engaged in discussions about the potential sell-off unilaterally, generating anger among nations and regions who feel it was done behind their backs.

But while there is a significant element of risk attached to this move, the chances of Infantino being brought down by it are slim, given how strong support is for him elsewhere.

Fifa would receive a huge influx of cash in one go if the plan is approved, and the proportion earmarked for national federations would be made available from 1 January 2027, according to a letter sent to each country by Infantino.

He added: "The decision whether or not to proceed with this proposal belongs entirely to you.

"In exchange, all that is required is your trust - everything else remains the same."

The appeal is clear - vote to help make us richer and we'll make you richer too.

But each World Cup makes significantly more money than the last - it will probably be worth far 

If Fifa sells stakes now, then the private investors will share in the rewards of that growth in the coming years, rather than Fifa and football doing so alone.

And ultimately, Fifa is a non-profit organisation under Swiss law, meaning its ultimate goal is - theoretically, at least - the long-term wellbeing of football rather than making a profit.

The big winners from the plan, then, would arguably be some of the smaller football nations, the private investors, and Infantino.

"What we know so far about how some national federations spend their money raises a lot of doubts about whether the money reaches the levels of football which Fifa promises," says Miguel Maduro, a former chairman of Fifa's governance committee.

Maduro claims he quit that role after 10 months because Infantino and Fifa's wider leadership disagreed with how the committee was operating.

"Fifa works as a political cartel - it is fed and supported on a system of patronage, that works through the money Fifa distributes to national federations. There have been cases of corruption," he added.

"There is a very high likelihood that this [proposal] will be approved.

"It is a form of legalised bribe."

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa for comment about Maduro's assessment.

Private equity investment has already transformed sports in the USA.

Rules have been changed in baseball, basketball, American football and ice hockey to allow for more minority investments in the past decade, causing team values to skyrocket.

And La Liga and Ligue 1 have already sold portions of their operations to private equity firm CVC Capital Partners in exchange for an immediate influx of money.

Infantino is hopping on a trend in sports economics rather than trying out something entirely new, but stands to further entrench his own power if he succeeds.

Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan

Uefa and PM criticise Infantino World Cup plan

Infantino's proposal has deepened his ongoing conflict with European governing body Uefa - the most powerful and wealthy regional organiser.

Uefa President Aleksander Ceferin boycotted the World Cup final in protest against Fifa's decision to overturn USA striker Folarin Balogun's suspension after an intervention from Trump.

That followed a series of Uefa announcements making clear it would not follow Fifa policy on controversial issues including dynamic ticket pricing and hydration breaks.

One of the cornerstones of the division between the two is that Fifa's revamped and expanded Club World Cup has become a clear, direct threat to Uefa's Champions League.

Previously Uefa was the only organisation which ran an international club football competition featuring the best players, watched by billions around the world and generating significant profits.

Last summer Fifa muscled in on that elite club football territory, adding teams from other continents to the mix.

Some national federations have expressed anger that they found out about the plans only when Fifa made them public, but crucially, many of the statements released so far have not explicitly condemned the concept of the sell-off itself.

That said, BBC Sport understands many Uefa members are angry about the plan and that a meeting is set to be convened for them to discuss a response.

On Tuesday Uefa said Fifa's plan is "to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends".

Some reports indicate a threat by European nations to boycott the World Cup could be possible. The theory is that a World Cup without European countries would severely compromise the tournament's value to Fifa.

But the chances of that coming to pass are debatable.

Europe is one of the main hosts of the next tournament in 2030, with Spain and Portugal holding the majority of matches alongside Morocco, and Spain is currently lobbying hard to win the right to host the final ahead of Morocco.

There is also a women's World Cup next year in Brazil, which could be an early target for any action, if Uefa does want to take a bold step of its own.

Uefa could potentially find and field a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year's presidential election, but given Uefa nations comprise only 55 votes, they would be unlikely to win.

If Ceferin and other European leaders really want to fight Infantino's plan as hard as possible, they must be willing to make a big move of some sort very quickly indeed.

For now, Infantino is as emboldened as he has ever been.

title: Why finger-clicking 'scandal' has gripped sporting world - Agnew
description: Why the wicketkeeper in the Saltburn Cricket Club 'finger-clicking' scandal is the key voice in any investigation.
fullText:
Everyone seems to have formed their own opinion on the alleged cheating scandal enveloping Saltburn Cricket Club, and it's not hard to see why.

I've had countless messages today from people who are intrigued by the whole thing. Many are from people who don't usually message me about cricket.

It's a perfect social media story which does the rounds very quickly and people quickly reach their own opinion.

At the centre of it all is the suggestion a second XI player from Saltburn Cricket Club, Brian Devine, clicked his fingers the moment the ball passed the bat of an opponent, thus making it sound like the ball had hit the edge.

Cricket scandal stories always grab people's attention and this one is the sort of incident in which people who are not interested in cricket can get involved – did he click his fingers or did he not? Could the umpire hear it or could he not?

It's one of those simple things that anybody can engage with. It's not as complicated as assessing whether a footballer has dived – this is a cut and dried thing that anybody can enter a debate into.

People seem to enjoy a Spirit of Cricket debate - it's part of the fabric of the game and almost unique to the sport.

Devine, who has been suspended by his club,, external must have a proper hearing and tell his side of the story. People have come to conclusions very quickly and maybe they're right but until there's been a proper investigation, it's difficult to pass judgement.

For me, the wicketkeeper, Josh Bowes, is the person who will ultimately know what happened. Unless Devine confesses to anything, the wicketkeeper is the star witness for the prosecution and the defence. It's up to him to be honest.

Bearing in mind all of us are reaching judgements from some pretty grainy video, if Devine is seriously managing to click his fingers so loudly the umpire can hear it outside, with everything else that is going on, then he clearly has to be punished.

Anybody who is caught cheating in any sport takes that risk. They take the risk of being exposed as a cheat and they'll be punished as a cheat.

Then there's the decision to be made about the team itself and whether other people knew about it and were part of it.

But that can only happen after there has been a proper hearing and proper process.

Let's be frank though, these things do happen in cricket - people are always pushing to try and gain an advantage. The only sport I am aware of where it doesn't happen, and I'd happily stand corrected here, is golf, because of its self-policing nature.

Whenever you have an umpire or referee to try and con as a player, then this sort of thing goes on.

In my playing days, I remember standing at first slip in a county match when West Indies fast bowler Andy Roberts was playing for us [Leicestershire].

The wicketkeeper at the time, who I won't name, ran on the spot very loudly in a distracting fashion as the bowler was running in. After he did it a couple of times, the batsman turned round and told him in no uncertain terms if he did it again, he would do something rather uncomfortable with his cricket bat.

We've had ball-tampering scandals – all of these things – and they all fall under the same bracket of foul play and bringing the game into disrepute.

What I would say is the whole Spirit of Cricket question is an incredibly difficult path to tread. These things happen and everybody has different views.

It starts with everybody having a different perspective or interpretation of the Spirit of Cricket and very few people agree on that. Then it kicks off from there. It's extraordinarily difficult to get a consensus on these things.

But it goes on everywhere, all around the world. I know it's been a big story in Australia too but I've played grade cricket in Australia and I think I'm pretty experienced in knowing how Australians play their grade cricket.

Their league cricket is utterly uncompromising, it's ruthless and I've certainly seen evidence of sharp practice in the two or three seasons I played there.

It's not the first incident and it won't be the last. What's important now is that we get a full and fair investigation.

Jonathan Agnew was talking to BBC Sport's Marc Higginson

title: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina
description: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over their behaviour after their World Cup final loss to Spain and throughout the tournament.
fullText:
Fifa has opened disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over their behaviour after their World Cup final loss to Spain and throughout the tournament.

Last week, the world governing body appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at the New York New Jersey Stadium, with multiple Argentina players and backroom staff involved in altercations with Spain players following their 1-0 loss in July.

On the recommendation of the prosecutor, Fifa will investigate Argentina players Nahuel Molina (two counts) and Leandro Paredes (three counts), and Argentina assistant coach Roberto Ayala (one count) for alleged assault under article 14 of Fifa's disciplinary code.

Molina may also face disciplinary action for one count of alleged unsporting behaviour under article 14.

Team-mate Thiago Almada and Spain midfielder Gavi are also accused of the same breach.

Under Fifa's disciplinary code, players and officials face at least a one-match suspension for unsportsmanlike conduct and at least three matches for assault.

Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble

Fifa 'assessing match reports' over Falklands banner

The Argentinian Football Association is facing disciplinary proceedings for potential breaches across multiple matches, including using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature (article 13), team misconduct (article 14), discrimination and racist abuse (article 15), and breaching order and security at matches (article 17).

The latter relates to discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, the team and spectators displaying inappropriate messages, and spectators throwing objects.

Argentina's players celebrated their semi-final win over England with a banner in support of their country's claim to the Falkland Islands. It read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", which translates as "The Falklands are Argentine".

title: Liverpool preparing opening bid for PSG's Barcola
description: Liverpool step up their interest for Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and are preparing an opening bid.
fullText:
Liverpool have stepped up their interest in Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and are preparing an opening bid.

Barcola, 23, has been identified as the primary option for Liverpool as they look to replace Mohamed Salah, who left at the end of last season.

The France winger is valued by PSG at around £145m. Such a fee would break the British transfer record but those at Anfield are keen on striking a deal closer to the £100m mark.

Barcola has two years left on his contract but is understood to be keen on a move to the Reds and a new challenge after falling down the pecking order at PSG.

Liverpool had initially wanted Yan Diomande but the RB Leipzig winger is now set to join Real Madrid.

We asked if you think the quotation for Barcola is a fair one. Here are some of your comments:

John: Truly flabbergasted at his price. Not denying his quality and potential but when you hear Vinicius Jr is valued at £137m you have to give your head a scratch.

Lee: He's proved his worth. A big signing for the new manager makes sense - get the season started with a buzz. Realistically we still need to look at the back four conundrum though.

Kate: I think it's scandalous the amount of money paid for these players! It's going up and up. If you want the best around then they know you'll pay but look what happened last season. I'm on the fence here, I do want Barcola but at that price, I think we should invest in quality, experienced defenders instead. We don't want a weak backline. Iraola knows how to get the best out of what we've got. We need defenders.

Andrew: Ridiculous amount of money. Can Barcola actually last a full 90 minutes? He seemed to be subbed between 60 and 70 mins. I hope that proves to be wrong if we buy him.

Paul: There appears to be enough attacking options already, surely last year showed the need is in defence. Make the back line solid and build out from there.

Stu: Barcola would be a good signing but he's not worth anywhere near £100m, never mind £145m. He's a squad player at PSG. If they won't accept £70m max then move on to someone else.

Dan: I happen to highly rate Barcola, one of those players who seems like he's been around for years and years then you realise he's only 23. During PSG's campaign anytime he was brought on he was a threat, maybe not the most polished finisher but a real threat and he has incredible pace as seen during France's World Cup run. Do I think he's worth £145m? Absolutely not. In today's market I'd have said between £60-£80m. A player with potential - young and fast but he's sat on PSG's bench all season.

fullText:
Tua Tagovailoa injury update: Latest news on Falcons QB being held out of training camp originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

When the Falcons signed Tua Tagovailoa, they gave themselves what they believed to be a good problem by entering 2026 with two starting-caliber quarterbacks on the roster.

As training camp gets underway, they instead have none.

Michael Penix Jr. hasn't been cleared for team drills, which is no surprise as he works his way back from ACL surgery, but a surprise injury to Tagovailoa has Atlanta reeling at the moment.

Here's the latest on Tagovailoa's status as camp gets underway.

MORE:Best free agents still available, from Stefon Diggs to Bobby Wagner

Tagovailoa won't practice yet after "something flared up" in his back, but head coach Kevin Stefanski said he expects the former Dolphins quarterback to return "shortly."

Stefanski says "something flared up" with Tagovailoa. "He's getting better and I expect him to be back shortly." #Falcons

— Marc Raimondi (@marcraimondi) July 29, 2026

ESPN's Adam Schefter reported Tagovailoa's injury is "not considered serious" and should have him back on the practice field "next week."

Still, Tagovailoa's absence has the Falcons' quarterback room in a dire place. Atlanta also released veteran Trevor Siemian due to a non-football injury on Wednesday, so Jack Strand, undrafted out of Minnesota State-Moorhead, is taking first-team reps at the moment.

The Falcons also signed former Cowboys and Ravens QB Cooper Rush on Wednesday for additional help.

MORE:See Tony Romo's arrest video

Tagovailoa is dealing with a back injury, though the ailment is "not considered serious," Schefter reports. Stefanski said Wednesday that the quarterback's back "flared up" but didn't offer many more details.

Tagovailoa is expected back on the practice field next week, according to Schefter, with Stefanski also saying he expects Tagovailoa to return "shortly."

The Falcons will undoubtedly remain cautious with both Tagovailoa and Penix, given their injury histories, but they are hoping to have both available in some capacity in the near future.

title: Cardinals have clear Dustin May, Ryne Stanek trade deadline plan
description: St. Louis is sticking to its early-season decision.
fullText:
Cardinals have clear Dustin May, Ryne Stanek trade deadline plan originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

This season was supposed to be a rebuilding year for the St. Louis Cardinals.

Yet, on July 29, they find themselves in the NL Wild Card race. The Cardinals are 2.5 games behind the Arizona Diamondbacks for the third and final Wild Card spot.

Surprise performances up and down the roster have helped the Cardinals reach this point, but they won't be making major trades at next week's deadline.

It may be the opposite. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal, Will Sammon and Katie Woo wrote Wednesday that the Cardinals are open to trading two of their impending free agent pitchers.

"When the St. Louis Cardinals signed Dustin May and Ryne Stanek over the offseason, they expected both veteran arms to help keep the team afloat in the first half," they wrote. "They also knew that with experienced starting and relief pitching always coveted at the deadline, they could easily flip both May and Stanek."

Reports indicate that St. Louis is sticking to that plan.

"That’s the plan for St. Louis, per multiple team sources briefed on the club’s thinking but granted anonymity to speak freely," The Athletic reported.

MORE: Giants willing to trade Heliot Ramos in big news for many MLB clubs

"Despite a surprisingly competitive first half, the Cardinals aren’t looking to deviate from president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom’s long-term outlook, which projects late 2027 or early 2028 as the team’s next competitive window."

May signed a one-year deal and has a 4.59 ERA in 20 starts. He has prior postseason experience with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Stanek also signed a one-year pact. The right-handed reliever has a 4.46 ERA in 40.1 innings but has held left-handed hitters to a .685 OPS.

title: Phillies Expect To Cut Struggling Slugger At Trade Deadline, ‘Hasn’t Been As Good’
description: Philadelphia Phillies manager Don Mattingly revealed plans to move a promising young outfielder as the trade deadline approaches.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies are in the final days before the MLB trade deadline searching for answers to an offense that has stalled at an inopportune time. After another frustrating series loss, pressure continues to mount on the front office to find upgrades capable of jump-starting a lineup with postseason aspirations.

Franchise slugger Bryce Harper recently made it clear that he believes reinforcements are necessary, and the numbers back him up. Philadelphia has struggled to generate consistent production from right field, making it one of the club's most glaring weaknesses as deadline decisions approach.

FORBES | By Peter Chawaga
Shohei Ohtani’s Ex-Interpreter ‘Loved’ Dodgers Before Deception Enabled Scandal

The Phillies appear ready to move on from rookie outfielder Gabriel Rincones Jr., who has struggled to seize an everyday opportunity despite receiving extended playing time against right-handed pitching.

On Tuesday, interim manager Don Mattingly acknowledged the club's growing concern over Rincones while explaining why Bryan De La Cruz has begun taking over regular duties in right field.

“Rico’s been given a decent runway against right-handed pitching,” Mattingly said, according to The Athletic’s Matt Gelb. “Hasn’t been as good as we’d like. De La Cruz, he’s getting his hits. And I know he’s going to be solid in the outfield and all that. So I don’t feel like it’s going to be worse than what we’re seeing.”

Gelb added that Mattingly’s comments were an indication that the team expects to cut Rincones from the major-league roster as the trade deadline approaches.

“They are onto a new everyday player there, De La Cruz, who started Tuesday against a righty for the first time,” Gelb added. “He was the only one in the lineup with two hits. He has supplanted rookie Gabriel Rincones Jr., who probably won’t be in the majors after the trade deadline. Mattingly said as much before Tuesday’s game.”

FORBES | By Peter Chawaga
Cardinals Cut Starter Immediately After Brutal Outing Against Cubs

The Phillies' offensive struggles have become impossible to ignore, particularly with the trade deadline just days away.

Harper, who is mired in an extended slump, offered a direct assessment of where the club stands.

“With the Philadelphia Phillies dropping their fourth straight series since the All-Star break, Bryce Harper was blunt when asked if the team needs reinforcements as the Monday trade deadline approaches,” ESPN reported. “‘I think we need some help,’ Harper said Tuesday night after the Phillies lost 1-0 to the Marlins, their eighth defeat in 11 games since the break. They have scored one run or fewer in six of those 11 games.”

If Philadelphia acquires another outfielder before the deadline — as many around baseball expect — the roster squeeze could leave Rincones without a place on the major league club. Mattingly's comments suggest that process may already be underway, with De La Cruz earning more opportunities while the Phillies evaluate external additions.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com
